title: The true bargain
hook: sent with twenty rupees to strike a good deal, he feeds hungry holy men and comes home empty-handed

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cobra's shade, the hood spread over a sleeping face. Your line was something shelters you. What did you thank? Day twenty-six.

Mehta Kalu has had enough. His son is a young man now, and he still hasn't shown the slightest interest in making money. The buffaloes wandered. The lessons turned into questions. So the father tries one more thing, the thing a practical man would try. He counts out twenty rupees, a real sum, puts it in his son's hand, and says: go to the market town. Buy something you can sell for more. Make a good deal. Bring back a profit. Show me you can do this. The son nods, takes the money, and sets off down the road. He does make a deal. Just not the one his father meant.
screen: `TWENTY RUPEES IN HIS HAND.` → `GO MAKE A GOOD DEAL.` → `NOT THE DEAL HIS FATHER MEANT.`

segments.voice: On the way, the story says, Nanak came across a group of holy men sitting by the road. Wandering ascetics, thin, quiet. He stopped and talked with them and found out they hadn't eaten in days. He looked at the twenty rupees. He thought about his father's words: make a good deal, a true one. And he went into the town and spent every coin on flour, lentils, butter and other food, brought it back and fed them all. Then he walked home with empty hands. Sacha sauda. Sacha means true. Sauda means a deal, a trade, a bargain. The true bargain. Nanak's answer to his father's instruction was that feeding the hungry was the truest deal there was. You didn't lose twenty rupees; you traded them for something that doesn't run out. His father didn't see it that way. The janamsakhis say Mehta Kalu was furious, and some tellings say he struck his son. Others in the family, and Rai Bular, stepped in to calm him. It's an honest touch in the story: the Guru's family didn't always understand him, and it hurt. Sikhs often see in this moment an early seed of the langar you met on day eight: food for anyone hungry, bought with honest money, given freely. And there's a gurdwara today called Sacha Sauda, in Pakistan, on the spot where tradition says the holy men were fed. Notice the clever thing about the story, too. Nanak didn't disobey his father's words. He obeyed them more deeply than his father intended. Make a true deal, the father said. So he did.
screen: `HOLY MEN WHO HADN'T EATEN IN DAYS.` · `SACHA — TRUE. SAUDA — A DEAL.` · `A FATHER WHO DIDN'T UNDERSTAND.` · `AN EARLY SEED OF THE LANGAR.` · then, large: `THE TRUE BARGAIN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and think about your money for a moment, without guilt. Where did it go this week? Coffee, rent, something online. Now imagine holding twenty dollars in your hand, just like Nanak held twenty rupees. Picture someone who's hungry: a stranger on your street, a neighbor who's struggling, a food bank shelf. Picture that twenty turning into a meal in their hands. Sit with how that deal feels. The bell holds the time.
Sacha sauda. The true bargain: twenty rupees traded for a meal for the hungry, the best deal Nanak could make.
Your line: the best bargain. Today, spend something small on someone hungry: a meal, a donation, a sandwich for a stranger. Day twenty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of sacha sauda as an early sign of the langar and of Guru Nanak's teaching on sharing; Gurdwara Sacha Sauda in Pakistan marks the place tradition connects with it.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: sacha (true) + sauda (a deal, a bargain).

trapdoor: what you thought: Nanak wasted his father's money.
what it means: he obeyed his father more deeply than intended: the truest deal was feeding the hungry.
what a scholar hears: the janamsakhis differ on the details. the story is sited at Chuharkana, now in Pakistan, where Gurdwara Sacha Sauda stands.
